Physiology-03.question: ১) Urine volume can be as low as ... L/day in a dehydrated person?
Physiology-03.exp:
In a dehydrated person, the body conserves water by increasing ADH secretion, which increases water reabsorption in the kidneys. As a result, urine volume can decrease to approximately 0.5 L/day.

Normal urine output:

  • Around 1–1.5 L/day in a normal adult

  • Minimum urine volume required for excretion of metabolic waste (obligatory urine volume) ≈ 0.5 L/day

Other options:

  • 1.0 L/day → Common normal value, not the lowest in dehydration

  • 1.5 L/day → Normal/high urine output

  • 2.0 L/day → Increased urine volume

Exam pearl:

  • Dehydration → ↑ ADH → ↑ Water reabsorption → ↓ Urine volume

  • Minimum urine volume ≈ 500 mL/day (0.5 L/day)

Physiology-03.question: ২) Hormones secreted by kidneys excludes
Physiology-03.exp:
The kidney secretes several hormones and hormone-like substances, including:

  • Erythropoietin (EPO) → Stimulates red blood cell production in bone marrow 

  • Prostaglandins → Produced in the kidney; regulate renal blood flow and sodium handling 

  • Thrombopoietin → Mainly produced by the liver (also small amounts from kidney) and involved in platelet production

  • Adrenalin (Epinephrine) → Secreted by the adrenal medulla, not the kidney 

Exam pearl:

  • Kidney endocrine functions:

    • Erythropoietin → RBC production

    • Renin → RAAS activation

    • Calcitriol (active vitamin D) → Calcium absorption

    • Prostaglandins → Renal regulation

  • Adrenal medulla → Catecholamines (Adrenaline + Noradrenaline)

Physiology-03.question: ৩) What is the basic differentiating point between plasma & ISF in case of composition?
Physiology-03.exp:
The basic differentiating point between plasma and interstitial fluid (ISF) is the protein content.

  • Plasma contains a high concentration of proteins (especially albumin, globulins, and fibrinogen) because proteins are retained within blood vessels. 

  • Interstitial fluid (ISF) has a very low protein concentration because most plasma proteins cannot pass through capillary walls.

Other options:

  • Cations → Similar composition in plasma and ISF (minor differences)

  • Anions → Similar, though chloride and bicarbonate may vary slightly

  • Phospholipid → Not the main distinguishing factor

Exam pearl:

  • Plasma vs ISF difference → Protein concentration

  • Plasma = blood fluid + proteins

  • ISF = plasma ultrafiltrate with very little protein

Physiology-03.question: ৪) Which is not a part of JG apparatus?
Physiology-03.exp:
The Juxtaglomerular (JG) apparatus is a specialized structure of the nephron that regulates renin secretion and blood pressure.

Components of JG apparatus:

  • Macula densa → Specialized cells of distal convoluted tubule that sense NaCl concentration

  • Juxtaglomerular cells (granular cells) → Modified smooth muscle cells of afferent arteriole that secrete renin

  • Extraglomerular mesangial cells (lacis cells) → Support signal transmission within JG apparatus

Bowman’s capsule is a part of the renal corpuscle and is not a component of JG apparatus.

Exam pearl:
JG apparatus = Macula densa + Juxtaglomerular cells + Extraglomerular mesangial cells
Main function → Renin secretion and regulation of GFR/BP

Physiology-03.question: ৫) The average blood volume of adults is about ... of body weight?
Physiology-03.exp:
The average blood volume in an adult human is approximately 7% of body weight.

Example:

  • A person weighing 70 kg has approximately 5 liters of blood.

  • Blood volume ≈ 70 mL/kg body weight (around 7%)

Other options:

  • 5% → Lower than normal blood volume

  • 9% → Higher than average

  • 10% → Not the normal value in adults

Exam pearl:

  • Adult blood volume = ~7% of body weight

  • Average blood volume = 5 L in a 70 kg adult

  • Plasma volume ≈ 55% of blood volume

Physiology-03.question: ৬) Highest capacity of reabsorption
Physiology-03.exp:
The Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT) has the highest capacity of reabsorption in the nephron.

Functions of PCT:

  • Reabsorbs about 65–70% of filtered Na⁺ and water

  • Almost 100% glucose and amino acids are normally reabsorbed

  • Reabsorbs bicarbonate, phosphate, and other solutes

Other options:

  • DCT (Distal Convoluted Tubule) → Fine regulation of electrolytes; less reabsorption than PCT

  • Loop of Henle (LOH) → Establishes medullary concentration gradient

  • Collecting duct (CD) → Regulates final urine concentration under ADH control

Exam pearl:

  • PCT = Maximum reabsorption site

  • Loop of Henle = Concentration of urine

  • DCT + Collecting duct = Hormonal regulation (aldosterone/ADH)

Physiology-03.question: ৭) The glomerular capillaries cannot filtrate...?
Physiology-03.exp:
The glomerular filtration barrier allows filtration of small molecules but normally prevents filtration of large plasma proteins (especially albumin).

Glomerular filtration:

  • Glucose → Filtered freely and normally reabsorbed in PCT

  • Sodium → Filtered freely

  • Creatinine → Filtered (and slightly secreted by tubules)

  • Plasma protein → Cannot pass through normal glomerular filtration barrier due to large size and negative charge

Exam pearl:

  • Normal urine should not contain significant protein

  • Proteinuria → Damage to glomerular filtration barrier

  • Filtration barrier = Fenestrated endothelium + Basement membrane + Podocyte slit diaphragm

Physiology-03.question: ৮) The percentage of TBW is highest in...
Physiology-03.exp:
The percentage of Total Body Water (TBW) is highest in newborns.

Approximate TBW as percentage of body weight:

  • Newborns → 70–75% (highest)

  • Adult male → ~60%

  • Adult female → ~50–55%

  • Elderly → ~45–50% (lowest due to increased body fat and reduced muscle mass)

Newborns have a higher water content because they have a greater proportion of extracellular fluid and less body fat.

Exam pearl:

  • TBW highest → Newborn

  • Adult male → ~60%

  • Adult female → ~50–55%

  • Elderly → ↓ TBW

Physiology-03.question: ৯) Blood is detected in urine by
Physiology-03.exp:
Blood (hemoglobin) in urine can be detected by the Orthotolidine test. This test is based on the peroxidase activity of hemoglobin, which produces a color change in the presence of hydrogen peroxide.

Other options:

  • Rothera’s test → Detects ketone bodies (especially acetone and acetoacetic acid) in urine

  • Hay’s surface tension test → Detects bile salts in urine

  • Fouchet’s test → Detects bilirubin in urine

Exam pearl:

  • Blood in urine → Orthotolidine test

  • Ketone bodies → Rothera’s test

  • Bile salts → Hay’s test

  • Bilirubin → Fouchet’s test

Physiology-03.question: ১০) Renal autoregulation is important to maintain the
Physiology-03.exp:
Renal autoregulation is the intrinsic ability of the kidney to maintain a relatively constant Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) despite changes in systemic blood pressure.

Mechanisms of renal autoregulation:

  • Myogenic mechanism → Afferent arteriole constricts or dilates in response to changes in pressure

  • Tubuloglomerular feedback → Macula densa regulates afferent arteriolar tone based on NaCl delivery

Other options:

  • RPF (Renal Plasma Flow) → Can change; not the primary function maintained by autoregulation

  • BP (Blood Pressure) → Mainly regulated by systemic mechanisms (RAAS, autonomic system)

  • Osmolarity → Controlled mainly by ADH and kidney concentrating mechanisms

Exam pearl:

  • Renal autoregulation → Maintains GFR

  • Effective between approximately 80–180 mmHg mean arterial pressure

  • Main mechanisms: Myogenic response + Tubuloglomerular feedback

Physiology-03.question: ১১) Which of the following is transported in intestinal epithelial cells by a Na+ dependent cotransport process?
Physiology-03.exp:
Alanine is absorbed from intestinal epithelial cells by a Na⁺-dependent cotransport mechanism (secondary active transport).

Intestinal absorption:

  • Amino acids (e.g., alanine) → Na⁺-dependent cotransport through amino acid transporters

  • Glucose and galactose → Na⁺-dependent cotransport via SGLT1

  • Fructose → Na⁺-independent facilitated diffusion via GLUT5

  • Fatty acids and triglycerides → Absorbed mainly by diffusion and transported as chylomicrons

Other options:

  • Fatty acids → Micelles → enterocytes → chylomicrons

  • Triglycerides → Broken down into fatty acids + monoglycerides before absorption

  • Fructose → Facilitated diffusion, not Na⁺ cotransport

Exam pearl:

  • Na⁺-dependent intestinal cotransport → Glucose, Galactose, Amino acids (Alanine)

  • Fructose → GLUT5 (Na⁺ independent)

  • Lipids → Chylomicrons via lymphatics

Physiology-03.question: ১২) Presence of positive benedict's test indicate that there might be a problem in
Physiology-03.exp:
A positive Benedict’s test in urine indicates the presence of reducing sugars (mainly glucose). Normally, glucose is completely reabsorbed in the Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT).

If the PCT is damaged or the glucose transport capacity is exceeded (e.g., diabetes mellitus), glucose appears in urine (glycosuria), producing a positive Benedict’s test.

Other options:

  • DCT → Mainly involved in fine regulation of electrolytes and acid–base balance

  • Loop of Henle (LOH) → Concentrates urine by establishing medullary osmotic gradient

  • Collecting duct (CD) → Regulates final urine concentration under ADH control

Exam pearl:

  • Glucose reabsorption site → PCT

  • Positive Benedict’s test → Glycosuria

  • PCT dysfunction → Loss of glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate in urine

Physiology-03.question: ১৩) Which step of urine formation occurs in glomerulus
Physiology-03.exp:
The glomerulus is the site where glomerular filtration occurs. Blood is filtered through the glomerular capillaries into Bowman’s capsule, forming the initial filtrate.

Steps of urine formation:

  • Glomerular filtration → Occurs in glomerulus

  • Tubular reabsorption → Occurs mainly in renal tubules (especially PCT)

  • Tubular secretion → Occurs in renal tubules (mainly DCT and collecting duct)

Other options:

  • Tubular reabsorption → Not a function of glomerulus

  • Tubular secretion → Not a function of glomerulus

  • All → Incorrect because only filtration occurs in glomerulus

Exam pearl:

  • Glomerulus → Filtration

  • PCT → Maximum reabsorption

  • DCT/Collecting duct → Secretion and fine regulation

Physiology-03.question: ১৪) Secretion of which of the following substances is inhibited by low pH?
Physiology-03.exp:
Low pH (acidic gastric contents) inhibits gastrin secretion through a negative feedback mechanism.

Mechanism:

  • When gastric pH falls below about 3, excess acid stimulates D cells in the stomach to release somatostatin.

  • Somatostatin inhibits G cells, causing ↓ gastrin secretion.

  • Reduced gastrin decreases gastric acid secretion.

Other options:

  • Secretin → Stimulated by low pH in duodenum; increases pancreatic bicarbonate secretion

  • CCK → Released mainly by fatty acids and amino acids in duodenum

  • VIP → Released from intestinal neurons; promotes intestinal secretion and smooth muscle relaxation

Exam pearl:

  • Low gastric pH → ↑ Somatostatin → ↓ Gastrin

  • Duodenal acid → ↑ Secretin → ↑ Bicarbonate secretion

Physiology-03.question: ১৫) Limiting pH of urine
Physiology-03.exp:
The limiting (minimum) pH of urine is approximately 4.5. The kidney can acidify urine up to this lowest pH to eliminate excess hydrogen ions.

Urine pH normally ranges:

  • 4.5 – 8.0

  • Average urine pH ≈ 6.0

Other options:

  • 3.5 → Too acidic; below the physiological limit

  • 4.0 → Below normal minimum urine pH

  • 5.0 → Can occur but is not the limiting value

Exam pearl:

  • Minimum urine pH = 4.5

  • Maximum urine pH = 8.0

  • Kidney maintains acid–base balance by H⁺ secretion and bicarbonate reabsorption.

Physiology-03.question: ১৬) Normal GFR is ....L/day?
Physiology-03.exp:
The normal Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is approximately 125 mL/min.

Daily calculation:

  • 125 mL/min × 60 min × 24 hours

  • ≈ 180 L/day

GFR represents the amount of filtrate formed by both kidneys per day.

Other options:

  • 125 L/day → Represents the rate value (mL/min) incorrectly converted

  • 625 L/day → Too high

  • 290 L/day → Incorrect value

Exam pearl:

  • Normal GFR = 125 mL/min = 180 L/day

  • Renal plasma flow ≈ 600–700 mL/min

  • Filtration fraction ≈ 20% (GFR/RPF)

Physiology-03.question: ১৭) Micelle formation is necessary for the intestinal absorption of
Physiology-03.exp:
Micelle formation is necessary for the intestinal absorption of fat-soluble substances, especially fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).

Bile salts form micelles in the small intestine, which help transport lipid-soluble molecules through the aqueous intestinal environment to the brush border of enterocytes.

Other options:

  • Galactose → Absorbed by Na⁺-dependent cotransport (SGLT1)

  • Leucine → Absorbed by amino acid transporters (Na⁺-dependent)

  • Bile acids → They themselves form micelles and are absorbed mainly in the terminal ileum, but are not the main substance requiring micelles for absorption

Exam pearl:

  • Micelles are essential for absorption of:

    • Fatty acids

    • Monoglycerides

    • Cholesterol

    • Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K)

  • Bile salts → Micelle formation → Lipid absorption

Physiology-03.question: ১৮) Kidney synthesize glucose by the process of
Physiology-03.exp:
The kidney synthesizes glucose by the process of gluconeogenesis, especially during prolonged fasting and starvation.

Gluconeogenesis:

  • Formation of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources such as:

    • Lactate

    • Glycerol

    • Glucogenic amino acids

  • Occurs mainly in the liver and also significantly in the renal cortex

Other options:

  • Glycolysis → Breakdown of glucose to produce energy

  • Glycogenesis → Formation of glycogen from glucose

  • Glucogenesis → Not a standard physiological term for glucose synthesis

Exam pearl:

  • Liver = major site of gluconeogenesis

  • Kidney cortex = important during prolonged fasting

  • Gluconeogenesis ↑ in starvation, cortisol excess, and diabetes mellitus

Physiology-03.question: ১৯) About what % of human body is fluid?
Physiology-03.exp:
Approximately 60% of an adult human body weight is fluid (Total Body Water, TBW).

Distribution of body fluid:

  • Total Body Water (TBW) → ~60% of body weight in adult male

  • Intracellular fluid (ICF) → ~40% of body weight (about 2/3 of TBW)

  • Extracellular fluid (ECF) → ~20% of body weight (about 1/3 of TBW)

Other options:

  • 40% → Represents mainly intracellular fluid, not total body fluid

  • 50% → Approximate TBW in adult females due to higher fat content

  • 65% → Higher than average adult value

Exam pearl:

  • Adult male TBW ≈ 60%

  • Adult female TBW ≈ 50–55%

  • Newborn TBW ≈ 70–75% (highest)

Physiology-03.question: ২০) Which of the following substances is secreted in response to an oral glucose load?
Physiology-03.exp:
Glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP) is an incretin hormone secreted from K cells of the duodenum and jejunum in response to an oral glucose load.

Actions of GIP:

  • Stimulates insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells in a glucose-dependent manner

  • Contributes to the incretin effect (greater insulin release after oral glucose compared with IV glucose)

Other options:

  • Gastrin → Secreted by G cells; stimulated by peptides, gastric distension, and vagal activity

  • CCK → Released in response to fats and amino acids; stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction

  • VIP → Secreted by intestinal neurons; increases intestinal secretion and relaxes smooth muscle

Exam pearl:

  • Oral glucose → GIP + GLP-1 → ↑ Insulin secretion

  • GIP = Incretin hormone from K cells

  • CCK = Fat digestion hormone

Physiology-03.question: ২১) Net filtration pressure in glomerulas (mmHg)
২২) To maintain normal H+ balance, total daily excretion of H+ should equal the daily
Physiology-03.option1: Fixed acid production plus fixed acid ingestion
Physiology-03.exp:
To maintain normal H⁺ balance, the amount of H⁺ excreted by the kidney must equal the amount of non-volatile (fixed) acid produced and ingested daily.

The body produces fixed acids mainly from:

  • Protein metabolism (sulfuric acid, phosphoric acid)

  • Dietary acid intake

The kidney maintains acid–base balance by:

  • Excreting H⁺ as titratable acids (mainly phosphate)

  • Excreting H⁺ as NH₄⁺ (ammonium)

  • Reabsorbing and generating HCO₃⁻

Other options:

  • HCO₃⁻ excretion → Normally very low; excessive loss causes acidosis

  • HCO₃⁻ filtered load → Most is reabsorbed, not equal to H⁺ excretion

  • Titratable acid excretion → Only one component of total renal H⁺ excretion

Exam pearl:

  • Daily H⁺ excretion = Daily fixed acid production + dietary acid load

  • Renal acid excretion = Titratable acid + NH₄⁺ excretion

  • HCO₃⁻ conservation is essential for maintaining blood pH

Physiology-03.question: ২৩) What is the normal value of fluid (ml) we get from metabolism?
২৪) Plasma & ISF are separated by
২৫) Organic substances excreted in urine excludes
২৬) Clearance rate is maximum for
Physiology-03.exp:
Inulin has the maximum clearance rate among the given substances because it is:

  • Freely filtered by glomerulus

  • Neither reabsorbed nor secreted by renal tubules

  • Completely excreted in urine

Therefore, inulin clearance = GFR and represents the ideal measure of glomerular filtration rate.

Other options:

  • Glucose → Normally completely reabsorbed in PCT, so clearance ≈ 0

  • Creatinine → Filtered and slightly secreted; clearance is close to GFR but slightly higher than true GFR

  • Sodium → Mostly reabsorbed, so clearance is low

Exam pearl:

  • Maximum clearance → PAH (because it is filtered + actively secreted → measures RPF)

  • GFR marker → Inulin (gold standard)

  • Creatinine → Clinically used estimate of GFR

Physiology-03.question: ২৭) Which part of renal tubule is never permeable to water?
২৮) Which decreases NaCl reabsorption?
২৯) Which prevents fall of GFR?
৩০) What is the value of renal plasma flow (ml/min)?
৩১) Maximum calories (/g) is derived from
৩২) Which of the following requires GLUT-5 transporter during absorption?
৩৩) Ptyalin is required in digestion of
৩৪) Secretion from which part of GIT lacks digestive enzyme
৩৫) Water content is least in
৩৬) Which one is acidic?
৩৭) Accessory digestive organs excludes
Physiology-03.exp:
Mouth (oral cavity) is part of the alimentary canal (GIT), not an accessory digestive organ.

Accessory digestive organs include structures that assist digestion but food does not pass through them:

  • Teeth → Mechanical digestion (chewing)

  • Tongue → Helps mastication, swallowing, taste

  • Salivary glands → Produce saliva containing digestive enzymes

Other options:

  • Teeth → Accessory organ

  • Tongue → Accessory organ

  • Salivary glands → Accessory organ

Exam pearl:

  • Alimentary canal: Mouth → Pharynx → Esophagus → Stomach → Intestine → Anus

  • Accessory digestive organs: Teeth, tongue, salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, pancreas

  • Mouth is NOT an accessory organ; it is a part of GIT

Physiology-03.question: ৩৮) Substance that increase salivary secretion
Physiology-03.exp:
Chloroform can increase salivary secretion by reflex stimulation of salivary glands through irritation of oral mucosa.

Other options:

  • Histamine → Mainly increases gastric acid secretion; not a major salivary stimulant

  • Ergotamine → Causes vasoconstriction and has no role in increasing saliva

  • Atropine → Decreases salivary secretion by blocking muscarinic receptors (causes dry mouth)

Exam pearl:

  • Parasympathetic stimulation → ↑ Salivary secretion (watery saliva)

  • Atropine → ↓ Saliva → Dry mouth (xerostomia)

  • Chloroform → Reflex salivary secretion stimulant

Physiology-03.question: ৩৯) Xerostomia means
Physiology-03.exp:
Xerostomia means dryness of the mouth due to reduced salivary secretion (hyposecretion).

Common causes:

  • Anticholinergic drugs (e.g., atropine)

  • Dehydration

  • Salivary gland disorders

  • Radiation therapy

Other options:

  • Wet mouth → Opposite condition

  • Excessive salivation → Called sialorrhea/hypersalivation

  • Absence of HCl → Related to gastric acid secretion, not saliva

Exam pearl:

  • Xerostomia = Dry mouth due to ↓ saliva

  • Atropine → blocks muscarinic receptors → xerostomia

Physiology-03.question: ৪০) Pepsinogen is activated by
Physiology-03.exp:
Pepsinogen is an inactive zymogen secreted by the chief cells of the stomach. It is activated into the active enzyme pepsin by hydrochloric acid (HCl) secreted from parietal cells.

Mechanism:

  • Pepsinogen + HCl → Pepsin (active enzyme)

  • Activated pepsin then digests proteins into peptides.

Other options:

  • Enterokinase → Activates trypsinogen into trypsin in the small intestine

  • Intrinsic factor of Castle → Required for vitamin B₁₂ absorption in the ileum

  • Trypsin → Activates pancreatic zymogens, not gastric pepsinogen

Exam pearl:

  • HCl → Activates pepsinogen → Pepsin

  • Enterokinase → Activates trypsinogen → Trypsin

  • Parietal cells → HCl + Intrinsic factor

  • Chief cells → Pepsinogen

Physiology-03.question: ৪১) Absence of intrinsic factor of castle may lead to
Physiology-03.exp:
Intrinsic factor of Castle is secreted by gastric parietal cells and is essential for the absorption of vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin) in the terminal ileum.

Absence of intrinsic factor leads to:

  • ↓ Vitamin B₁₂ absorption

  • Impaired DNA synthesis in RBC precursors

  • Formation of large abnormal RBCs (megaloblastic anaemia)

  • This condition is called pernicious anaemia

Other options:

  • Iron deficiency anaemia → Due to iron deficiency, not intrinsic factor deficiency

  • Haemolytic anaemia → Due to increased RBC destruction

  • Sideroblastic anaemia → Due to defective haem synthesis

Exam pearl:

  • Intrinsic factor + Vitamin B₁₂ → Ileum absorption

  • Intrinsic factor deficiency → Pernicious anaemia

  • Parietal cells secrete: HCl + Intrinsic factor

Physiology-03.question: ৪২) Factor stimulating the Secretion of Hydrochloric Acid
Physiology-03.exp:
Gastrin is the major hormone that stimulates secretion of hydrochloric acid (HCl) from the parietal cells of the stomach.

Mechanism:

  • Food (especially proteins) → stimulates G cells in the stomach

  • G cells release gastrin

  • Gastrin stimulates:

    • Parietal cells → ↑ HCl secretion

    • ECL cells → ↑ Histamine release → further ↑ HCl secretion

Other options:

  • Secretin → Inhibits gastric acid secretion and stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion

  • Gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP) → Inhibits gastric acid secretion and slows gastric motility

  • Peptide YY → Reduces gastric secretion and motility

Exam pearl:

  • Gastrin → ↑ HCl secretion

  • Histamine (H₂ receptor) → ↑ HCl secretion

  • Secretin + GIP → ↓ gastric acid secretion

Physiology-03.question: ৪৩) Source of Pepsinogen
Physiology-03.exp:
Pepsinogen is secreted by the chief cells (zymogenic cells) of the stomach.

  • Chief cells produce pepsinogen, an inactive enzyme precursor.

  • In the presence of HCl from parietal cells, pepsinogen is converted into active pepsin.

  • Pepsin digests proteins into peptides.

Other options:

  • Parietal cell → Secretes HCl and intrinsic factor

  • G cell → Secretes gastrin

  • EC cell (enterochromaffin cell) → Secretes serotonin and helps regulate GI motility

Exam pearl:

  • Chief cell → Pepsinogen

  • Parietal cell → HCl + Intrinsic factor

  • G cell → Gastrin

  • ECL cell → Histamine

Physiology-03.question: ৪৪) Which of the following substances is released from neurons in the GI tract and produces smooth muscle relaxation?
Physiology-03.exp:
Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) is released from neurons of the enteric nervous system and causes smooth muscle relaxation in the gastrointestinal tract.

Functions of VIP:

  • Relaxes GI smooth muscle

  • Relaxes sphincters (e.g., lower esophageal sphincter)

  • Stimulates intestinal secretion of water and electrolytes

  • Causes vasodilation

Other options:

  • Secretin → Secreted by duodenum; stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion and inhibits gastric acid secretion

  • Gastrin → Increases gastric acid secretion and gastric motility

  • CCK → Stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction

Exam pearl:

  • VIP = "Vasodilator + Intestinal secretion + Paralysis/relaxation of smooth muscle"

  • Gastrin → ↑ HCl

  • Secretin → ↑ HCO₃⁻

  • CCK → ↑ Pancreatic enzymes + Gallbladder contraction

Physiology-03.question: ৪৫) Which of the following is the site of secretion of intrinsic factor?
Physiology-03.exp:
Intrinsic factor of Castle is secreted by the parietal cells (oxyntic cells) located mainly in the gastric fundus and body of the stomach.

Function:

  • Intrinsic factor binds with vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin)

  • Helps absorption of vitamin B₁₂ in the terminal ileum

  • Deficiency causes pernicious anaemia

Other options:

  • Gastric antrum → Contains G cells that secrete gastrin

  • Duodenum → Site of bicarbonate secretion and digestion, not intrinsic factor secretion

  • Ileum → Absorbs vitamin B₁₂–intrinsic factor complex

Exam pearl:

  • Parietal cell (fundus/body) → HCl + Intrinsic factor

  • Intrinsic factor deficiency → Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency → Pernicious anaemia

  • Terminal ileum → Absorption of B₁₂–intrinsic factor complex

Physiology-03.question: ৪৬) Which one is gold standard for measurement of GFR
Physiology-03.exp:
Inulin clearance is the gold standard for measurement of GFR (Glomerular Filtration Rate).

Reason:

  • Inulin is freely filtered by the glomerulus.

  • It is not reabsorbed and not secreted by renal tubules.

  • Therefore, the amount of inulin excreted in urine exactly reflects the amount filtered by the kidney.

Other options:

  • Sodium clearance → Not used for measuring GFR because sodium is extensively reabsorbed.

  • Creatinine clearance → Clinically used to estimate GFR, but slightly overestimates GFR due to tubular secretion.

  • Urea clearance → Not accurate because urea is partially reabsorbed.

Exam pearl:

  • Gold standard GFR measurement → Inulin clearance

  • Clinical estimation of GFR → Creatinine clearance/eGFR

  • Renal plasma flow measurement → PAH clearance

Physiology-03.question: ৪৭) Uric acid is the metabolic waste product of
Physiology-03.exp:
Uric acid is the end product of purine metabolism, which comes from the breakdown of nucleic acids.

Pathway:

  • Nucleic acids → Purine bases (adenine, guanine) → Hypoxanthine → Xanthine → Uric acid

Other options:

  • Protein → Breakdown produces urea (main nitrogenous waste)

  • Creatine → Breakdown produces creatinine

  • Haemoglobin → Breakdown produces bilirubin (from heme portion)

Exam pearl:

  • Uric acid → Purine/nucleic acid metabolism

  • Urea → Protein metabolism

  • Creatinine → Creatine phosphate metabolism

  • Bilirubin → Haemoglobin breakdown

Physiology-03.question: ৪৮) Specific gravity of urine is low in
Physiology-03.exp:
Specific gravity of urine is low in Diabetes insipidus due to inability of the kidney to concentrate urine.

Mechanism:

  • ↓ ADH secretion (central DI) or ↓ renal response to ADH (nephrogenic DI)

  • ↓ Water reabsorption in collecting ducts

  • Produces large volume of dilute urine (polyuria)

  • Urine specific gravity becomes very low (usually <1.005)

Other options:

  • DM (Diabetes mellitus) → Specific gravity is usually high due to glucose in urine (glycosuria)

  • CRF (Chronic renal failure) → May cause isosthenuria (fixed specific gravity around 1.010)

  • AKI (Acute kidney injury) → Variable changes depending on tubular function

Exam pearl:

  • Low urine specific gravity → Diabetes insipidus

  • High urine specific gravity → Diabetes mellitus

  • Isosthenuria (≈1.010) → Chronic renal failure

Physiology-03.question: ৪৯) Presence of which particle in urine indicates UTI?
Physiology-03.exp:
Presence of nitrite in urine is an important indicator of urinary tract infection (UTI).

Mechanism:

  • Many UTI-causing bacteria (especially Gram-negative bacteria like E. coli ) convert nitrate → nitrite using bacterial nitrate reductase enzyme.

  • Therefore, a positive urine nitrite test suggests bacterial infection.

Other options:

  • Glucose → Suggests diabetes mellitus or renal glycosuria

  • Protein → May indicate renal disease, inflammation, or transient proteinuria

  • Bile salt → Seen in obstructive jaundice or cholestasis

Exam pearl:

  • UTI marker in urine → Nitrite (+) and leukocyte esterase (+)

  • Most common UTI organism → E. coli

Physiology-03.question: ৫০) Digestion of proteins starts in
Physiology-03.exp:
Protein digestion starts in the stomach by the action of pepsin.

Mechanism:

  • Gastric parietal cells secrete HCl, which converts pepsinogen → pepsin (from chief cells).

  • Pepsin begins the breakdown of proteins into smaller peptides.

Other options:

  • Mouth → No significant protein digestion (only mechanical breakdown)

  • Small intestine → Major site of protein digestion by pancreatic enzymes (trypsin, chymotrypsin, peptidases)

  • Large intestine → Mainly absorbs water and electrolytes; minimal bacterial metabolism

Exam pearl:

  • Protein digestion starts → Stomach (pepsin)

  • Carbohydrate digestion starts → Mouth (ptyalin/salivary amylase)

  • Fat digestion mainly occurs → Small intestine (pancreatic lipase)
